title: Comparing Distributed-Memory Programming Frameworks with Radix Sort
problem: Distributed-memory programming frameworks vary significantly in their capabilities for managing communication and synchronization overhead, making it difficult to evaluate trade-offs between scalability, productivity, and performance.
motivation: Software developers need guidance on selecting distributed-memory programming frameworks based on empirical performance data for communication-intensive workloads across supercomputer architectures.
method: Ran distributed radix sort—an algorithm that constantly moves data between computers, making it a tough test for any framework—on five programming frameworks (Chapel, MPI, OpenSHMEM, Conveyors, Lamellar) on HPE Cray systems. For each framework, they measured three things: raw speed, how well it scaled to more computers, and how much code was needed to implement it. By testing all five on the exact same demanding problem, they could see which frameworks handled communication overhead best and which were easiest to program.
key_novelty: This benchmark directly compares five distributed-memory programming frameworks on identical communication-intensive tasks, measuring practical trade-offs in performance, scalability, and code complexity.
contributions: Empirical performance comparison of five distributed-memory programming frameworks
Code metrics showing Chapel achieves 113 SLOC for radix sort implementation
Performance data: 17 billion elements/second on 128 nodes of HPE Cray Supercomputing EX
Open-source implementations enabling reproducibility and community optimization
limitations: Evaluation limited to single algorithm (radix sort); results may not generalize to other communication patterns or computation-bound workloads.
